title: The Ginninderra tragedy: a ghost story etched in Canberra's history
excerpt: They say two stockmen still wander the banks of Ginninderra Creek.
content:
I'm tip-toeing softly on the red granite path, making sure it doesn't make a crunch, but I'm not sure why.

Ahead my torch beam catches the outline of a white-winged chough perched on the edge of a wooden bridge. He's silent but his beady eyes are fixed on me.

A couple more steps forward and I realise why. He's on watch for all his mates, for suddenly a flock of about 15 of the crow-like birds start to screech chaotically, flying en masse from the canopy of one tree to another. Argh! They are above. Behind. All around me. Now I know what it must have been like on the set of Alfred Hitchcock's The Birds.

Eventually they let me through, their eyes now glowing red in my torchlight, continuing to watch my every step.

This rickety footbridge, hidden in Palmerville Heritage Park near McKellar, which spans an arm of the Ginninderra Creek has a spooky reputation. And I can see why. It's only mid-afternoon. I can only imagine what it's like walking through here during the witching hour.

With relics dating back to the convict era buried in nearby earthen mounds, English elms, oaks and poplars creating thickets so dense they turn day into night, it reminds me of the woods, home to ancient graves and witches covens, that often feature in television shows like Midsomer Murders.

The bridge across a backwater of the Ginninderra Creek at Palmerville near where George Kemp and Edward Crace drowned in 1892. Picture by Tim the Yowie Man

Indeed, this secluded part of Palmerville boasts its own folklore - with reports of shadowy figures and even the apparition of two stockmen seen wandering here. Sound far-fetched? Surely it's just the mind playing tricks. Possibly. However, I'm just a stone's throw from a double-drowning dating from the late nineteenth century. A real tragedy, not one made-up for Detective Chief Inspector Tom Barnaby to investigate.

It was a late afternoon in September 1892 and Edward Crace, master of nearby Gungahlin Homestead, who also owned Ginninderra Estate (Palmerville), had just been visiting the Ginninderra Homestead (since demolished but in the Palmerville precinct).

With him was his coachman, 23-year-old George Kemp.

Partly obscured by pine trees, the entrance to Gungahlin Homestead, left. At right, the south-facing wing of Gungahlin Homestead with its bay windows. Picture by Tim the Yowie Man

A big storm hit causing the Ginninderra Creek to rise rapidly.

Back then there were no bridges, and travellers relied on low-level crossings or fords.

However, both nearby crossings were in flood.

Store owner George Harcourt (yes, after whom the modern pub is named) had warned Crace to be careful where to cross, and to use the wider and shallower 'Store Crossing', but Crace, known for being pigheaded, took no notice.

Entrance to the old Coach House at Gungahlin Homestead. This is where Edward Crace was headed when he and his groom George Kemp drowned in Ginninderra Creek. Picture by Tim the Yowie Man

Kemp wasn't keen on crossing either. In fact, some reports suggest Crace "took the reins from his young coachman" and demanded, "we will try the 'Garden Crossing' because it is much shorter that way".

With waters continuing to rise, the horse became trapped in the swirling currents and Kemp dived in to try and calm it. But he was soon swept under the water. So too the horse.

Crace remained high and dry in the coach - in the middle of the creek, that is - until it eventually toppled over, spilling him also into the raging torrent.

According to newspaper reports of the time, Crace's body was found about midnight "about half a mile downstream".

However, despite an extensive search for Kemp, he couldn't be found. With the creek still in flood, rescuers used poles, hooks, rakes, hooks, grappling irons and whatever they could get their hands on to probe miles of the waterway downstream. But it was in vain.

Two days later when Crace was buried in the family plot at St John's Church (in Reid), Kemp's body still hadn't been found.

In fact, it wasn't for another seven days that Kemp's body was retrieved from the creek, found trapped in submerged roots very close to where he had originally gone under while trying to steady the horse.

The news of where he was found was no surprise to Samuel Shumack, author of Tales and Legends of Canberra Pioneers (ANU Press, 1967), for he apparently had a dream soon after the mishap "that Kemp's body was in a deep channel where the drowning accident took place".

The day after his dream, Shumack even told leader of the search party, Senior Constable Loughlan, of his premonition but it was dismissed.

"He laughed and said, 'Forty young men searched that channel on Sunday - a sucking pig could not remain there unobserved as every inch of it was searched under my supervision.'"

The graves of George Kemp and Margaret Reid at St Johns in Reid. Picture by Tim the Yowie Man

The double tragedy sent shockwaves through the small tight-knit community, especially hard on both Kemp's fiancé Margaret McPherson (Shumack's wife's cousin) and Crace's wife, Kate, who was left to manage the massive estate amid the onset of the economic depression of the late 1890s.

There was widespread public sympathy for Kemp, who, having emigrated from Scotland, had no family in the new colony. His bravery was widely praised in local newspapers, contrasting his selfless actions with the perceived recklessness of his master. In fact, it was his fellow servants at Gungahlin who raised funds for the significant sandstone headstone that adorns his grave.

The graves of George Kemp and Margaret Reid at St Johns in Reid. Picture by Tim the Yowie Man

Some years after Kemp's death Margaret caught the eye of Thomas Reid, a groom employed at Duntroon where Margaret worked. Eventually they married. But still, Margaret placed flowers the grave of her first true love every Sunday. She also requested to be buried in the same grave as him, a wish her husband honoured when she died in 1940.

Stories of premonition, tragedy and eternal love aren't just scripted for television shows, they unfold in real life. Even in our very own backyard.

Peek in Gungahlin Homestead

On Saturday, April 11 2026, from 10am to 2.30pm the National Trust (ACT) is hosting an open day at Gungahlin Homestead - former home of Edward Crace who after buying the 1862-65 Georgian-style two-storey home in 1877 added the Victorian-style sandstone extension.

View of Gungahlin Homestead from the south-west c.1890. Picture supplied

There will be tours, stalls, entertainment and refreshments, so bring the family.

Oh, and be sure to ask your guide to show you where the homestead's fixed phone was located - apparently it was the district's first private line.

Crace Business Park, 80 Bellenden Street, Crace, ACT. Entry is by donation.

Looking down the grand staircase in the Victorian-era extension to Gungahlin Homestead. Picture by Tim the Yowie Man

Creepy cellar

There are stories that convicts were locked up in the cellar. However, given it was built decades after the convict era, I suspect the real purpose of the bars was to protect the cellar's sought-after liquid content.

The bars on its windows have led some to erroneously claim that convicts were kept locked-up in Gungahlin Homesteads cellar. Picture by Tim the Yowie Man

George Kemp Memorial

A park that serves as a memorial to Kemp is located near the corner of Narden Street and Digby Circuit in Crace.

George Kemp Park in Crace. Picture by Tim the Yowie Man

Palmerville Heritage Loop

A recently completed 1.2km loop connects existing trails with a new 600-metre path featuring raised boardwalks and gravel. Be sure to check out the oaks and elms in the area which are among the oldest in Canberra. Access via Owen Dixon Drive, McKellar. While the convict-era structures at Palmerville were sadly long-ago (1950s and earlier) bulldozed, there are still some tangible reminders of Palmerville's built past, including a historic water trough.

Picnic group at the ruins of the old convict barracks of Palmerville Station, Gininnderra, c. 1915. Picture by Hall Heritage Centre

Palmerville 200

Palmerville 1826, a Bicentennial Exhibition, launches at 12.30pm on Sunday, April 12 at the Hall Heritage Centre and will be open each Sunday (12-4) and Thursday (10-12) throughout April. Highlights include a display visualising the Palmer-Campbell-Murray Sunday dinner held at the homestead on January 23, 1848 (after the shearing) and an audio-visual tour of the property from 1826 to 1876.

Children outside Craces Gungahlin homestead, c. 1890. Picture by Hall Heritage Centre

Last week: Did you recognise this two-storey house? Picture supplied

Last week: Congratulations to Alan Fitzgerald of Hughes who was first reader to correctly identify last week's photo as an 1898 photo of Glebe House which once stood near present-day Glebe Park in Civic.

Unfortunately, unlike Gungahlin Homestead which is still standing and which we can appreciate on historic tours, Glebe House was demolished in the 1950s. When built in 1873, as the rectory for nearby St John's Church, the two-storey home was one of the most prestigious homes in the district. However, after the compulsory acquisition of the land by the Commonwealth in the early 1900s, the home was subsequently used as part of a school and later a guesthouse. In 1954 it was sold by tender to the Acton Football Club on the proviso it be demolished to make way for Cooyong Street and growing numbers of motorists. This was undertaken by volunteers from the football club who also cleaned the beautiful clay bricks and reused them to build the new club house in Franklin Street, Forrest. Does anyone know if it's still there?

This 1898 photo features the Reverend Pierce Gallard Smith's family preparing to leave home for an outing on horseback. If you look closely, you might be able to make out in the foreground the family's pet cockatoo on top of its wooden fruit box shelter.

You can discover the former site Glebe House on a special Canberra & Region Heritage Festival event on April 19 in which good friend of this column Tony Maple will lead you through Canberra's past and present. Starting at the St John's Schoolhouse exhibition, learn about the challenges posed to early colonial buildings in the face of rapid city growth then follow an easy 1.7km guided walk tracing the shift from 19t-century pastoral flats to a bold mid-century city. Finish with afternoon tea back at the St Johns Schoolhouse Museum. Bookings essential. For more info: events@nationaltrustact.org.au
